name: Server Hardware Variability
description: Subtle differences in CPU clock speeds, memory latency, and network bandwidth between the two servers can cause asynchronous delays in coin flips and counter updates. These slight variations can manifest as distinct latency groups due to the random nature of the protocol.

name: Network Latency Variation
description: Network latency between the controller and each server is unlikely to be perfectly constant.  Fluctuations in network congestion, routing, and jitter contribute to uneven delays in message transmission, creating latency peaks and troughs that are reflected in the observed multimodal distribution.

name: Coin Generation Algorithm Precision
description: The algorithms used by the servers to generate the coin flip result (heads/tails) might not be perfectly uniform or truly random. Subtle biases or variations in the pseudorandom number generators (PRNGs) can introduce timing differences that manifest as latency groups.

name: Controller Processing Latency
description: The time taken by the controller to make decisions (selecting which server to query and updating the counter) isn't constant.  Factors like the complexity of the decision logic or load on the controller itself contribute to latency variation.

name: Server Load/CPU Utilization
description: If either server is experiencing higher CPU utilization or other processes are competing for resources, the coin flip generation and counter update operations will be slower, leading to latency fluctuations. This is especially impactful if the PRNG is affected.

name: Memory Access Patterns
description: The way the servers access memory (for storing the counter and the PRNG state) can introduce timing differences, especially under load. Variations in cache hits and misses will lead to inconsistent delays.

name: System Clock Drift
description: Even slight differences in the system clocks of the two servers can cause them to process events at slightly different times, contributing to timing variations and observed latency patterns.

name: Network Packet Loss/Corruption
description: Small amounts of packet loss or data corruption during network transmission can lead to retransmissions, significantly increasing latency and generating distinct latency clusters.  This is exacerbated by variable network conditions.

name: Coin Flip Decision Delay (Server)
description: The time it takes a server to actually make the coin flip decision and generate the heads/tails result is not a perfectly fixed delay. This could be due to internal scheduling within the server, impact of other processes, or caching effects.

name: Interference (EM)
description: Electromagnetic interference, particularly if the servers are in an environment with sensitive electronics, could potentially introduce timing jitter in the clock signals and affect the hardware components involved in the coin flip process.

name: Thermal Throttling
description: If server temperatures exceed thresholds, the system may throttle clock speeds to prevent overheating. This introduces predictable but variable delays in processing.

name: Operating System Scheduling Variations
description: Variations in OS scheduling algorithms, even if the overall CPU usage is similar, can cause different levels of priority for the coin flip and counter update tasks.

name: Cache Contention
description: If both servers are heavily using memory, competition for cache lines can increase access times and lead to latency variations.

name: Software Library Timing
description: The efficiency of the software libraries used for PRNG and data manipulation could be subject to variations and/or implementation dependent timing issues.

name: Network Queueing Delay
description: The queues used to buffer network packets can introduce delays, especially under load. These queues are not always constant and can exhibit varying levels of congestion.
